title: The mobile visit for an architecture studio
metaTitle: The mobile visit to an architecture studio
excerpt: Most clients will judge an architecture practice on a phone. The first screen still has to show built work, name the constraint, and start a project conversation.
alt: Curved library shelves packed with books, seen from a balcony, a tall wall of work that only stays legible if you can still find one volume.
caption: A wall of books from the balcony. The small screen still has to make one project legible. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What must the first phone screen contain?
faqs.answer: A recognizable piece of built work, the constraint in a sentence, and a way to start a project conversation. If any of those three sit below the fold because a desktop crop was preserved, the phone page is unfinished. The menu can wait. Those three cannot.

faqs.question: Should we design the desktop page first?
faqs.answer: Design the phone first for this audience, then let the wide screen add breathing room. A cinematic desktop composition that collapses into an abstract band on a phone has let the wrong device decide. Wide screens can have more margin. They should not have a different argument.

faqs.question: How do we judge whether the phone visit is good enough?
faqs.answer: Walk outside with a mid-range phone and try to retell the first project, then start a conversation. Check that the main image arrives quickly and the page does not jump as it loads. If you need the office monitor to understand the building, the visit is still a desktop visit.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
An architecture studio mobile website is the version most clients will actually judge. They are comparing offices on a phone, often away from a desk. The first screen still has to show built work, with the constraint named, and a way to start a project conversation. Do not let the desktop composition decide the phone page.

If the wide layout needs a paragraph of explanation before the building makes sense, the phone will not get that paragraph. It will get a crop and a thumb. Design for that.

## The phone is the review

Assume the first look is outdoors, one-handed, with glare. The client has two other practices open in tabs. Nielsen Norman Group’s research on [how long people stay on web pages](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) found that the first 10 seconds are when people decide whether to stay, and that a clear value proposition in those seconds is what earns a longer look. On a phone, those seconds are one screen, not a scroll.

The value proposition is still the building plus the constraint. "Alteration behind a retained facade" next to a photograph of that facade. Not a logo, not a film, not a manifesto in 11-pixel type. If the sentence does not fit, shorten the sentence. Do not move it below the image and hope they scroll.

[web.dev’s Web Vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals) ask you to judge the experience at the 75th percentile, split by mobile and desktop. A page that feels instant on the studio iMac and late on a phone has not passed. Largest Contentful Paint should occur within 2.5 seconds. Interaction to Next Paint should be 200 milliseconds or less. Cumulative Layout Shift should be 0.1 or less. Those are the numbers to hold the hero, the menu, and the captions to.

Treat the phone as the primary deliverable in the scope. Desktop is the same argument with more room. When a stakeholder review happens only on a laptop, you will approve the wrong crop. Put a phone on the table in every review.

## The first screen, specified

Specify the first screen in writing before anyone opens a layout file.

- One photograph of built work, cropped so the building or the room is recognizable at the width of a phone.
- The project name and one sentence naming the constraint.
- A text action: Start a project. The same words as everywhere else.
- The practice name, small, not instead of the project.

That is the screen. A second project can sit just below. A film can sit later, with a caption and without sound. Awards can sit later still.

Test the crop by covering the sides of the desktop frame with your hands. If the subject disappears, you need a separate art-directed crop, not a smaller version of the wide file. Many elevations only work wide. On a phone, switch to the court, the door, or the room where the decision is visible. The constraint sentence must match the crop the phone shows. Do not describe a retaining wall that the phone has sliced off.

Type has to be readable without pinch-zoom. If the caption is the proof, it cannot be a whisper under a full-bleed image. Give it contrast against the photograph or, better, place it on a solid ground beside or below the image. WCAG contrast is a quality bar here even before it is a compliance conversation. Pale type on a dusk sky fails both.

The action must be tappable. Leave space around it. Do not park it under a browser chrome guess. Sticky headers that eat a third of a phone are how the constraint falls off the screen. A short header with the action is enough.

## Desktop must not overrule this

Designers fall in love with the wide composition because the building finally fits. Keep that composition for wide screens. Do not let it dictate the document order. The phone order is the order of the content: image, constraint, action, next project. Wide screens can place the caption beside the image. They should not introduce a different story.

Beware components that only reveal the sentence on hover. Phones do not hover. If the project name appears only when a cursor enters, the mobile visit is a silent gallery. Put the name in the page.

Beware horizontal carousels as the only way to see three projects. Some clients will swipe. Many will not. Stack the three. A swipe can be an extra, not the library.

Beware video headers that autoplay. They cost data, they shove the sentence down, and they often fail to show the building until several seconds in. If you keep a film, start it on a user gesture, below the first proof.

Review desktop second. Ask only: does the wide screen keep the same facts, with better comfort? If the desktop version adds a manifesto above the projects, delete it in both layouts. Do not maintain two arguments.

## Tap, type, and motion

The menu was covered as labels. On the phone it is also a target. Items need space. The project list should be text links or cards with real headings, not a mosaic of untitled crops. A mosaic is a desktop souvenir.

Forms must be usable with the phone keyboard. The right input types, a visible label, and errors that say what to fix. A contact path that works in a desktop preview and breaks on a phone keyboard is a lost job. Keep the fields few. Address and a note. The client is already on a small screen.

Motion should explain, then get out of the way. A short fade when an image arrives is plenty. A sequence that delays the caption until a scroll timeline finishes is the desktop composition winning again. Respect reduced motion. Hanabi treats that as part of the craft on a marketing site, with Motion used where it helps and a quieter state where someone asks for less. The building does not need a parallax to be serious.

Buttons should not wait on a script before they can be tapped. Interaction to Next Paint is the measure of that wait. Decorative libraries that block the main thread will fail a client who taps Start a project twice and thinks the site is dead.

## Images that arrive, layouts that stay

Give every image its width and height, or an equivalent aspect ratio, so text does not jump when the file loads. That jump is layout shift, and on a phone it can move the button as the thumb arrives. Reserve the space. Then load a file sized for the phone, not the print original.

The hero is the likely Largest Contentful Paint element. Compress it for the display size. A separate, tighter crop for small screens often weighs less and communicates more. Test on a slow connection once. You do not need a lab for the first verdict. If you are staring at a blank screen long enough to wonder, the client has already left.

Captions should be in the HTML, directly under or beside the reserved space, so they are present even while the image resolves. The argument should not depend on the photograph having finished.

Do not inject a cookie wall, a newsletter modal, or an awards popup over the first screen. On a phone those cover the only proof you had. If you need a notice, put it where it does not hide the building.

## A pass you do on the pavement

The review is a walk. Load the page on a phone that is not the one you designed on. Retell the first project in one sentence. Tap through to a second project. Start the conversation path and stop before you submit, unless you are testing a staging form. Note where your thumb hesitates.

Do this for the homepage, one project page, the people page, and the contact path. Those are the pages this client strings together. A perfect homepage with a project page that is a desktop PDF scan is a failed visit.

Fix crops before you add pages. A short site that works on a phone will beat a long site that only works in the studio. When you want a reference for projects told at a readable scale, look through [selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). Notice which constraint you can still retell on a small screen. That is the bar. Hanabi designs and builds with that phone pass in the scope, in Next.js, so the crops and the sentences can be corrected after launch without a new poster.

Write down the three failures you found and fix those before any new animation. Most mobile problems on architecture sites are crop, contrast, and a missing sentence. They are not a lack of features.

## What they do when they are ready

A good first screen creates a reply. The client wants to know what happens if they reach out, how soon, and what to have ready. If that answer is buried in a ten-field form, the phone visit ends in a shrug.

The next piece is [a contact path for an architecture studio](/blog/a-contact-path-for-an-architecture-studio). Design it for the same phone. The building got their attention. The path has to be just as clear as the caption.
